questions.question: A badminton academy has 8 seniors (average height 165.5 cm) and 3 juniors (average height 149.33 cm). The correct average height of all 11 trainees is ____ cm.
questions.hint: Use (165.5 × 8 + 149.33 × 3) ÷ 11, not the mean of the two averages.
questions.explanation: Example 1. (1324 + 448) ÷ 11 = 1772 ÷ 11 = 161.09 cm. Method 1 (mean of averages) is wrong because the groups have different sizes.

questions.question: In Example 1, two methods are used to find the group average. The method that gives the correct average height is ____.
questions.hint: The overall average is the total of all heights divided by 11.
questions.explanation: Example 1. Method 2 adds all 11 heights and divides by 11. Method 1 treats the two group averages equally, which is wrong here.

questions.question: The sum of the 8 senior heights is equal to 165.5 × 8, which is ____ cm.
questions.hint: Average × number of values = sum.

questions.question: Method 1 failed for the badminton heights because the two groups have ____.
questions.hint: A simple mean of averages works only when the collections are the same size.
questions.explanation: There are 8 seniors and 3 juniors, so the senior average must get more weight.

questions.question: Jaspreet cycled 5 weekdays each week for 3 weeks. The weekly averages are 12.8, 15.8 and 18 minutes. The mean time per weekday over the 3 weeks is ____ minutes.
questions.hint: Each week has 5 days, so the mean of the three weekly averages is correct.

questions.question: Method 1 (mean of weekly averages) worked for Jaspreet’s cycling because each week has ____ cycling days.
questions.hint: Equal collection sizes make the mean of averages equal to the overall mean.
questions.explanation: Example 2. Each week has 5 weekdays, so the three averages can be treated equally.

questions.question: Two glasses have equal amounts of lemonade, one with 10% jaggery and the other with 20% jaggery. After mixing, the jaggery concentration is ____ %.
questions.hint: Equal quantities: the mixture concentration is the ordinary mean.

questions.question: A 500 mL lemonade with 10% jaggery is mixed with 200 mL lemonade with 20% jaggery. The jaggery concentration of the mixture is about ____ %.
questions.explanation: Example 4. (50 + 40) ÷ 700 = 90/700 ≈ 0.13, so about 13%. Closer to 10% because the bowl is larger.

questions.question: In Example 4, the quantity of jaggery in the 500 mL of 10% lemonade is ____ mL.
Brass batch A is 200 kg with 70% copper. Batch B is 120 kg with 50% copper. Batch C is 45% copper. The combined alloy is 55% copper. The weight of Batch C is ____ kg.
In Example 5, the mass of copper in the 200 kg batch that is 70% copper is ____ kg.
Rehmat scored 60%, 64% and 73% in internals, project and final. If the three parts are weighted equally, her annual Maths score is ____ %.
questions.hint: Ordinary mean of the three percentages.

questions.question: Rehmat scored 60%, 64% and 73%. The annual score uses weights 3 : 2 : 5. Her annual Maths score is ____ %.
Section A (30 students) has average 72. Section B (25 students) has average 76. The combined average of both sections is ____.
Three equal quantities of fertiliser have nitrogen fractions 1/10, 9/50 and 3/60. The fraction of nitrogen in the mixture is ____.
questions.hint: Mean of the three fractions (equal quantities).

questions.question: A goldsmith melts 9 units at 12 varṇa, 5 units at 10 varṇa and 17 units at 11 varṇa. The purity of the combined gold is ____ varṇa (2 d.p.).
questions.hint: Weighted mean of the varṇa values.

questions.question: Average daily rainfall is 3.5 mm (May), 10 mm (June) and 8.7 mm (July). Which expression gives the combined daily average? (Use 31, 30, 31 days.)
questions.hint: Weight each monthly average by the number of days in the month.
questions.explanation: Exercise 10.1 Q4. May and July have 31 days, June has 30. Combined average = (3.5×31 + 10×30 + 8.7×31) ÷ 92.

questions.question: 100 mL kashayam with 5% spice, 200 mL with 10% spice and 300 mL with 15% spice are combined. The spice concentration is ____ % (2 d.p.).
300 mL kashayam with 5% spice, 200 mL with 10% spice and 100 mL with 15% spice are mixed. The spice concentration is ____ % (2 d.p.).
questions.hint: The 5% batch is now the largest, so the mix is closer to 5%.

questions.question: A customer rates food 5, service 3 and ambience 4. Weights are 4 : 3 : 2. The combined restaurant rating is ____ (2 d.p.).
Savitri scored 35/50 (internals), 44/60 (project) and 80/100 (final). Weights 3 : 4 : 5. Which expression(s) give her annual score as a percentage?
questions.hint: Convert each part to a percentage (or to a fraction of that paper) before applying the weights.
questions.explanation: Exercise 10.2 Q1. (i) uses raw marks. (ii) divides raw marks by 100. (iii) uses 35/50, 44/60, 80/100 then ×100. (iv) converts each to a percentage first. Both (iii) and (iv) are correct.

questions.question: A shop sold books for ₹8000 at 30% profit and covers for ₹1000 at 50% profit. The profit percentage on total sales is ____ % (2 d.p.).
questions.hint: Total profit ÷ total sales × 100.

questions.question: A stork’s average over 20 days is 44.5 km per day. On day 21 it flew 55 km. The average over 21 days is ____ km.
600 mL of 5% salt is mixed with 300 mL of 8% sugar. The salt concentration in the mixture is ____ % (2 d.p.).
questions.hint: Only the first solution contains salt. Total volume 900 mL.

questions.question: 600 mL of 5% salt is mixed with 300 mL of 8% sugar. The sugar concentration in the mixture is ____ % (2 d.p.).
questions.hint: Only the second solution contains sugar.
questions.explanation: Exercise 10.3 Q3. Sugar = 300×0.08 = 24 mL. 24/900 = 0.0267 → 2.67%. (Option (v) in the book.)

questions.question: 10 litres of pani has 8% spice. Regular water is added so the spice becomes (3/4) of the original concentration. The volume of water to add is ____ litres.
questions.hint: New concentration = 6%. Spice amount stays 0.8 L.

questions.question: Fitness marks use weights 4 : 5 : 6 for strength, flexibility, agility. Rashi scored 60, 65, 70. Keerthi scored 55, 65, 75. Who has the greater weighted total?
questions.hint: Keerthi is 5 lower on the smallest weight and 5 higher on the largest weight.
questions.explanation: Exercise 10.3 Q5(i). The +5 on agility (weight 6) outweighs the −5 on strength (weight 4).

questions.question: Rashi scored 60, 65 and 70 with weights 4 : 5 : 6. Her final mark is ____ (2 d.p.).
Keerthi scored 55, 65 and 75 with weights 4 : 5 : 6. Her final mark is ____ (2 d.p.).
Ten customers rated food, ambience and service (table). Mean food rating is ____.
Using the same restaurant table, the mean ambience rating is ____.
Using the same restaurant table, the mean service rating is ____.
Food, ambience and service means are 4.3, 3.3 and 2.8. Combined with weights 6 : 5 : 4, the average rating is ____ (2 d.p.).
Male langurs average 16.5 kg, females 13.8 kg, all langurs 14.925 kg. Without calculating, there are ____.
questions.hint: The overall mean is closer to the female mean.
questions.explanation: Exercise 10.3 Q7. 14.925 is closer to 13.8 than to 16.5, so there are more females.

questions.question: Male mean 16.5 kg, female mean 13.8 kg, combined mean 14.925 kg, x males and y females. Which equation is correct?
questions.hint: The combined mean is the weighted mean of the two group means.
questions.explanation: Exercise 10.3 Q7(i). Expression (a) is the definition of the combined average.

questions.question: 60 langurs have combined average 14.925 kg. Males average 16.5 kg and females 13.8 kg. The number of male langurs is ____.
35 female langurs average 13.8 kg. One more female of 15.2 kg is admitted. The new female average is ____ kg (2 d.p.).
25 male langurs average 16.5 kg. Two males of 16.9 kg and 16.1 kg are released. The new male average is ____ kg.
questions.hint: The two released males average 16.5 kg, so the remaining mean is unchanged.
questions.explanation: Exercise 10.3 Q7(iv). Sum = 412.5. Remove 33. Remaining 379.5 ÷ 23 = 16.5 kg.

questions.question: 25 male langurs average 16.5 kg. One male loses 1 kg. The new male average is ____ kg.
questions.hint: The total mass falls by 1 kg; the count stays 25.

questions.question: 1 litre of Dead Sea water (≈34% salinity) is mixed with 2 litres of purified water (≈0.001% salinity). The mixture salinity is about ____ %.
Can Dead Sea water (34%) and purified water (0.001%) be mixed to match groundwater salinity (0.01%)?
options: Yes, but only with 1 L each
questions.hint: A mixture concentration always lies between the two ingredient concentrations.
questions.explanation: Exercise 10.3 Q8(ii). 0.01% is between 0.001% and 34%, so yes.

questions.question: How many litres of purified water (0.001%) should be mixed with 1 litre of Dead Sea water (34%) to reach groundwater salinity 0.01%? About ____ litres.
Can Dead Sea water (34%) and groundwater (0.01%) be mixed to get purified-water salinity (0.001%)?
options: Yes, add a lot of groundwater
No — 0.001% is smaller than both ingredients
questions.hint: You cannot go below the smaller of the two concentrations.
questions.explanation: Exercise 10.3 Q8(iii). 0.001% < 0.01% < 34%, so it is impossible.

questions.question: From Table 10.2, the family that spent the least on housing is Family ____.
questions.hint: Compare the Housing column.
questions.explanation: Table 10.2 Q1. C spent ₹950, the smallest housing amount.
questions.chart: THIS QUESTION REQUIRES A FIGURE UPLOAD — cluster-column charts of Table 10.2 (also solvable from the table).

questions.question: From Table 10.2, the family that spent the most on healthcare is Family ____.
questions.hint: Compare the Healthcare column.
questions.explanation: Table 10.2 Q2. A spent ₹1770 on healthcare.

questions.question: Family A’s education expenditure is ____ rupees.
questions.hint: Read Family A, Education.

questions.question: The category on which Family B spent the most is ____.
questions.hint: Compare Family B’s six amounts.
questions.explanation: Table 10.2 Q4. Housing ₹1750 is Family B’s largest spend (recreation is 0).

questions.question: Family A spent more on ____ than on food.
questions.hint: Food 1700 vs healthcare 1770.

questions.question: The family that spent the least overall is Family ____.
questions.hint: Add all six categories for each family.
questions.explanation: Table 10.2 Q6. A = 8425, B = 7286, C = 7040. Family C is least.
questions.chart: THIS QUESTION REQUIRES A FIGURE UPLOAD — stacked bar of Table 10.2 (also solvable by adding the table).

questions.question: Family C’s total expenditure is ____ rupees.
questions.hint: Add C’s six category amounts.

questions.question: The percentage of Family C’s expenses that were on housing is ____ % (1 d.p.).
Which family has the smallest share of total expenditure on healthcare?
questions.hint: Compare healthcare ÷ total for each family.
questions.chart: THIS QUESTION REQUIRES A FIGURE UPLOAD — 100% stacked bar / pie charts of Table 10.2.

questions.question: On the IUCN stacked column, the number 14,234 on top of the 2019 column represents ____.
options: the total animal species on the Red List in 2019
questions.hint: The top of a stacked column is the sum of all classes that year.
questions.explanation: Exercise 10.4 Q1(i). 14,234 is the total of all animal classes listed in 2019.
questions.chart: THIS QUESTION REQUIRES A FIGURE UPLOAD — stacked columns of IUCN Red List species by class, 2007–2019, totals 7851 to 14234.

questions.question: The IUCN chart total in 2007 is 7,851 and in 2019 is 14,234. The increase in the listed animal-species count is ____.
questions.hint: Subtract the 2007 total from the 2019 total.
questions.chart: THIS QUESTION REQUIRES A FIGURE UPLOAD — IUCN stacked columns with labelled totals.

questions.question: From the IUCN stacked column, the number of reptile species on the list in 2016 is approximately ____.
questions.hint: Read the height of the reptile (red-brown) band on the 2016 column (total 12,630).
questions.explanation: Exercise 10.4 Q1(ii). The reptile band is the second slice from the bottom; it is about 1,200 species.
questions.chart: THIS QUESTION REQUIRES A FIGURE UPLOAD — IUCN stacked columns; estimate the reptiles band on the 2016 column.

questions.question: Between 2007 and 2019 on the IUCN chart, which class(es) show a relatively small increase?
questions.hint: Compare the height of each colour band in 2007 with 2019.
questions.explanation: Exercise 10.4 Q1(iii). The mammal and bird bands stay almost the same height; insects, fish, amphibians and others grow much more.
questions.chart: THIS QUESTION REQUIRES A FIGURE UPLOAD — IUCN stacked columns 2007 vs 2019.

questions.question: A bowler took 62 Test, 100 ODI and 32 T20 wickets at home. Wickets taken at home in all formats together are ____.
questions.hint: Add the Home row.

questions.question: The same bowler took 172 Test, 49 ODI and 71 T20 wickets overseas. Overseas wickets in all formats are ____.
questions.hint: Add the Overseas row.

questions.question: Test wickets (home + overseas) are ____.
questions.hint: Add the Test column.

questions.question: ODI wickets (home + overseas) are ____.
questions.hint: Add the ODI column.

questions.question: T20 wickets (home + overseas) are ____.
questions.hint: Add the T20 column.

questions.question: A house used 360 + 300 + 120 + 220 kWh in 2005. The total daily-category consumption for 2005 is ____ kWh.
questions.hint: Add the four 2005 category values.

questions.question: In 2005, lighting was 360 kWh out of 1000 kWh. Lighting’s share is ____ %.
In 2005, cooling was 300 kWh out of 1000 kWh. Cooling’s share is ____ %.
In 2005, kitchen appliances were 120 kWh out of 1000 kWh. Their share is ____ %.
In 2005, other appliances were 220 kWh out of 1000 kWh. Their share is ____ %.
In 2025 the category values are 220, 800, 460 and 520 kWh. The 2025 total is ____ kWh.
questions.hint: Add the four 2025 values.

questions.question: In 2025, lighting is 220 kWh out of 2000 kWh. Lighting’s share is ____ %.
In 2025, cooling is 800 kWh out of 2000 kWh. Cooling’s share is ____ %.
In 2025, kitchen appliances are 460 kWh out of 2000 kWh. Their share is ____ %.
In 2025, other appliances are 520 kWh out of 2000 kWh. Their share is ____ %.
A 100% stacked bar shows Fatima 50%–30%–20% and Naveen 40%–35%–25% (summer–monsoon–winter). Which statement can be inferred?
options: Fatima had more blooms in summer than in monsoon
In summer Fatima had more blooms than Naveen
In winter Fatima had fewer blooms than Naveen
Both gardens had the same total flowers
Winter had the most flowers in both gardens
The two gardens had equal summer blooms
questions.hint: Percents can be compared inside one bar, not across bars, unless totals are known.
questions.explanation: Example 8. (i) is within Fatima’s garden, so it is true. (ii)–(iv) need actual totals, which a 100% bar does not give.
questions.chart: THIS QUESTION REQUIRES A FIGURE UPLOAD — 100% stacked bars for Fatima and Naveen by season.

questions.question: From a 100% stacked bar alone, can we decide which garden had more flowers in summer?
options: No, because summer is never shown
Yes, the longer summer percent wins
No — we need each garden’s total
questions.hint: A larger percentage of a smaller total can still be fewer flowers.
questions.explanation: Example 8 Case 1 vs Case 2: Fatima’s summer % is higher, but her actual summer count can be larger or smaller.

questions.question: The average Indian spends 34% of the day sleeping. That is ____ hours (2 d.p.).
questions.hint: 34% of 24 hours.
questions.chart: THIS QUESTION REQUIRES A FIGURE UPLOAD — 100%/24h strip of an average Indian’s day.

questions.question: Paid work is 13% of the average Indian’s day. That is ____ hours (2 d.p.).
questions.hint: 13% of 24 hours.
questions.chart: THIS QUESTION REQUIRES A FIGURE UPLOAD — average Indian’s day strip.

questions.question: Fig. 10.5 / 10.6 is both a stacked bar and a 100% stacked bar because every stack totals ____ hours.
questions.hint: A full day is 24 hours, so each stack is 100% of a day.
questions.explanation: The text: each stacked bar’s total is the same, 24 hours.

questions.question: A T20 team scored 6 runs in over 1 and 12 runs in over 2. The run rate after 2 overs is ____.
questions.hint: Total runs ÷ overs so far.

questions.question: After 19 overs the run rate is 6. The team scores 12 in the 20th over. The run rate after 20 overs is ____.
questions.hint: Runs after 19 overs = 6×19 = 114. Then (114+12)÷20.

questions.question: Five friends collected 6, 4, 5, 4 and 4 shuttlecock prices. Their averages are ay, as, ak, ap, ag. The combined average is ____.
questions.hint: Weight each friend’s average by how many prices that friend collected.

questions.question: There are 13 nylon and 10 feather shuttlecock prices, with averages an and af. The overall average price is ____.
questions.hint: Weight each type’s average by its count.
questions.explanation: EOE Q2(ii). (13an + 10af) ÷ 23. This equals the combined average from Q2(i).

questions.question: Shreyas holds 25 shares at ₹150 each and buys 10 more at ₹30. His new average price per share is ____ rupees (2 d.p.).
Vaishnavi holds 5 shares at ₹150. She buys n shares at ₹30 and her new average is ₹70. The number of shares she bought is ____.
A 30-hasta pool is in 5 sections of lengths 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 hastas and depths 9, 7, 7, 3, 2 hastas. The mean depth is ____ hastas.
questions.hint: Weighted mean of depths, weights = section lengths.

questions.question: Suvarna has 1 g gold bought at ₹15k. She buys 1 g more at ₹30k. The new average price is ____ thousand rupees per gram.
Suvarna has 1 g at ₹15k and buys 2 g at ₹30k. The new average price is ____ thousand rupees per gram.
Suvarna has 1 g at ₹15k and buys 1 g at ₹10k. The new average price is ____ thousand rupees per gram.
Suvarna has 1 g at ₹15k and buys 10 g at ₹10k. The new average price is ____ thousand rupees per gram (2 d.p.).
Suvarna has 1 g at ₹15k and buys 0.5 g at ₹30k. The new average price is ____ thousand rupees per gram.
Suvarna has 1 g at ₹15k and buys 0.5 g at ₹15k. The new average price is ____ thousand rupees per gram.
questions.hint: Same price, so the average stays 15.

questions.question: If every weight in a weighted average is doubled, the weighted average ____.
questions.hint: The factor 2 cancels in numerator and denominator.

questions.question: From the objects-orbiting-Earth graph, the total number of objects in 2003 was about ____.
questions.hint: Read the stacked total just after the year 2000.
questions.explanation: EOE Q7(i). The 2003 stack is about 8,000 objects.
questions.chart: THIS QUESTION REQUIRES A FIGURE UPLOAD — cumulative objects orbiting Earth; read ~8000 in 2003.

questions.question: From the objects-orbiting-Earth graph, the total of about 8,000 objects in 2003 had roughly doubled (to about 16,000) by the year ____.
questions.hint: Find the year when the stacked total is about twice the 2003 total.
questions.explanation: EOE Q7(i). Read the stacked total near 16,000 — around 2016 on the printed chart (approximate).
questions.chart: THIS QUESTION REQUIRES A FIGURE UPLOAD — cumulative objects orbiting Earth, payload vs other, 1960–2025.

questions.question: The map shows the percentage of schools with a playground. Which statement(s) can be inferred?
options: (a) only — Haryana has more playground-schools than Uttarakhand
(c) only — Punjab has the highest number of playground-schools
(b) and (d) — Arunachal is about 2/3, and Maharashtra (93%) with more schools than Telangana (74%) has more playground-schools
questions.hint: A larger percentage is not a larger count unless the totals are known. 93% of a larger school-count beats 74% of a smaller one.
questions.explanation: EOE Q8(i). (a) and (c) confuse share with count. (b) Arunachal ≈ 68% ≈ 2/3. (d) MH 93% and more schools than TG 74% ⇒ more playground-schools. Valid: (b) and (d).
questions.chart: THIS QUESTION REQUIRES A FIGURE UPLOAD — India map of % of schools with a playground (Arunachal 68%, Haryana 90%, Uttarakhand 78%, Punjab 98%, Maharashtra 93%, Telangana 74%).

questions.question: On the playground map, the percentage of schools with a playground in Arunachal Pradesh is ____ %.
questions.hint: Read the label on Arunachal Pradesh (far north-east).
questions.explanation: EOE Q8. The map shows 68%, which is about 2 out of 3 schools.
questions.chart: THIS QUESTION REQUIRES A FIGURE UPLOAD — playground-percentage map; Arunachal Pradesh labelled 68%.

questions.question: Can the nationwide percentage of schools with a playground be found from the state-wise percentage map alone?
options: No, because maps are never numeric
Yes, if the map is to scale
No — we also need the number of schools in each state
Yes, use the largest state only
questions.hint: A national weighted mean needs each state’s school count as the weight.
questions.explanation: EOE Q8(ii). Extra information needed: number of schools (or enrolment) in each state.
questions.chart: THIS QUESTION REQUIRES A FIGURE UPLOAD — playground-percentage map.

questions.question: Three athletes’ triathlon split times (hh:mm) are given. To see who finished first and compare actual segment times, the better chart is a ____.
questions.hint: Finishing time is a total of actual minutes, not a share of 100%.
questions.explanation: EOE Q10(i). A stacked bar shows actual durations and the total; a 100% bar hides who was faster.

questions.question: If only a 100% stacked bar of the triathlon splits is drawn, which question can be answered?
options: The clock time of the start
About what fraction of Athlete 1’s time was cycling?
Which athlete took the longest for running?
questions.hint: A 100% bar shows shares of each athlete’s own total, not the totals themselves.
questions.explanation: EOE Q10(ii). Only (b) is a within-bar fraction. (a) and (c) need actual times.

questions.question: Athlete 1’s splits are 1 h 8 min, 5 h, and 3 h 15 min. The total race time is ____ minutes.
questions.hint: Convert each split to minutes and add.

questions.question: If every weight in a weighted average is increased by 1 (not multiplied), the weighted average ____.
options: moves closer to the ordinary (unweighted) mean
questions.hint: Adding the same constant to every weight mixes the old weighted mean with the ordinary mean.
questions.explanation: EOE *Q15. New mean = (Σ(w+1)x)/(Σw + n) = (Σwx + Σx)/(W+n), a blend of the old weighted mean and the ordinary mean.

questions.question: A farm was 60% cows, 25% sheep, 15% chickens. All three animal counts then decreased. Which change in shares is impossible?
options: cows % down, sheep % up, chickens % same
all three percentages stay the same
cows % up, sheep % up, chickens % down
cows % down, sheep % up, chickens % up
questions.hint: The three shares must still add to 100%.
questions.explanation: EOE *Q16. (i) all three percentages decreasing is impossible. (ii) all increasing is also impossible. (iii)–(v) can happen depending on how much each count fell.

questions.question: After all three animal populations fall, can all three percentage shares stay exactly 60%, 25% and 15%?
options: Only if the total is 100 animals
Yes, if each count falls in the same ratio
questions.hint: Equal relative change leaves shares unchanged.
questions.explanation: EOE *Q16(iii). If each group is multiplied by the same factor k < 1, the percentages stay the same.

questions.question: The sum of the 3 junior heights is equal to 149.33 × 3, which is about ____ cm.
questions.hint: Average × count = sum.

questions.question: In Example 4, the quantity of jaggery in the 200 mL of 20% lemonade is ____ mL.
In Example 5, the mass of copper in the 120 kg batch that is 50% copper is ____ kg.
In Case 1 of Example 8, Fatima’s garden had 210 flowers in the year and 50% bloomed in summer. The number of summer blooms in Fatima’s garden is ____.
questions.chart: THIS QUESTION REQUIRES A FIGURE UPLOAD — Case 1 stacked bar: Fatima 105–63–42 (total 210), Naveen 48–42–30 (total 120).

questions.question: In Case 1 of Example 8, both gardens had 42 blooms in one season, but the percentages were different. Those 42 blooms are ____ % of Naveen’s 120 flowers.
questions.explanation: Example 8 Case 1. 42/120 = 35% (Naveen’s monsoon). Fatima’s 42 winter blooms are 20% of 210.

questions.question: Given a stacked bar chart with actual totals, can we always draw the corresponding 100% stacked bar chart?
options: Yes — divide each part by that bar’s total
Only if all totals are equal
Only if there are three bars
No, unless we also have a pie chart
Yes, but only for percentages already given
No, because lengths cannot be scaled
questions.hint: Each part’s share is (part ÷ bar total) × 100.
questions.explanation: Think and Reflect after Example 8 / chapter summary: stacked → 100% stacked is always possible.

questions.question: Given only a 100% stacked bar chart (no actual totals), can we recover a unique stacked bar of actual counts?
options: No — many different totals give the same 100% bar
Yes, if there are two bars
questions.hint: The same percentages can come from 100 flowers or 10,000 flowers.
questions.explanation: Think and Reflect / chapter summary: 100% stacked → stacked is not possible without the totals.

questions.question: Leisure, social and travel take 27% of the average Indian’s day. That is ____ hours (2 d.p.).
questions.hint: 27% of 24 hours.
questions.chart: THIS QUESTION REQUIRES A FIGURE UPLOAD — average Indian’s day strip; leisure 27%.

questions.question: On Fig. 10.6, children (6–14) spend ____ % of the day sleeping.
questions.hint: Read the green sleep band for children.
questions.explanation: Fig. 10.6. Children sleep 38% of the day.
questions.chart: THIS QUESTION REQUIRES A FIGURE UPLOAD — age-wise 100% stacked time-use; children sleep band 38%.

questions.question: On Fig. 10.6, children (6–14) spend ____ % of the day on learning.
questions.hint: Read the learning (grey) band for children.
questions.explanation: Fig. 10.6. Children learning 22%. Youth learning drops to 11%.
questions.chart: THIS QUESTION REQUIRES A FIGURE UPLOAD — age-wise time-use; children learning 22%.

questions.question: On Fig. 10.6, youth (15–24) spend ____ % of the day on learning.
questions.hint: Read the learning band for the youth column.
questions.explanation: Fig. 10.6. Youth learning 11% (much less than children’s 22%).
questions.chart: THIS QUESTION REQUIRES A FIGURE UPLOAD — youth learning band 11%.

questions.question: The nylon-and-feather combined average (13a_n + 10a_f)/23 equals the five-friends combined average. The two expressions are ____.
options: equal — both are the mean of all 23 prices
equal only if all friends collected the same number
questions.hint: Both expressions add up every listed price and divide by 23.
questions.explanation: EOE Q2(ii). Yes — they are two groupings of the same 23 prices, so the overall means match.

questions.question: Athlete 2’s splits are 1 h 5 min, 5 h 10 min, and 3 h 35 min. The total race time is ____ minutes.
questions.hint: Convert each split to minutes and add.

questions.question: Athlete 3’s splits are 1 h 22 min, 5 h 55 min, and 3 h 50 min. The total race time is ____ minutes.
questions.hint: Convert each split to minutes and add.

questions.question: Using the three totals 563 min, 590 min and 667 min, the athlete who finished first is Athlete ____.
questions.hint: The smallest total time wins.
questions.explanation: EOE Q10. Athlete 1 has the smallest total, 563 minutes.

questions.question: After all three animal populations fall, can all three percentage shares increase at once?
options: Yes, if cows fall the most
Yes, if chickens fall the least
Yes, if the total falls by 10%
Yes, if each count falls by 1
No, unless one share is zero
No — the three shares must still add to 100%
questions.hint: If every share rose, the sum would exceed 100%.
questions.explanation: EOE *Q16(ii). All three percentages increasing is impossible, just as all three decreasing is impossible.

questions.question: Cows were 60%, sheep 25%, chickens 15%. All counts fell. Can cows’ share fall, sheep’s share rise, and chickens’ share stay 15%?
options: Yes — if cows fall faster than sheep, chickens can stay the same share
No, shares cannot change when counts fall
questions.hint: Shares can move in different directions as long as they still add to 100%.
questions.explanation: EOE *Q16(iv). Possible: e.g. cows fall a lot, sheep fall a little, chickens fall in the same ratio as the new total.

questions.question: Cows were 60%, sheep 25%, chickens 15%. All counts fell. Can both cows’ and sheep’s shares rise while chickens’ share falls?
options: Yes, only if sheep become zero
Yes — if chickens fall much faster than cows and sheep
No, because two shares cannot rise
questions.hint: Two shares can rise if the third falls by the same total percentage points.
questions.explanation: EOE *Q16(v). Possible when the chicken count drops by a larger relative amount.

other objects grew steadily; payload stayed almost flat then rose sharply after about 2015
